contributions.headingText: Anal squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is a malignant epithelial tumour characterized by origin from the anal mucosa, keratin production, intercellular bridges, and frequent HPV infection.
2C00.3 & XH0945 Squamous cell carcinoma of anus or anal canal & Squamous cell carcinoma
Anal SCC is localized in the anus.

Anal SCC generally presents with symptoms and signs related to the presence of a mass, such as discomfort, discharge, and haemorrhage. Clinical examination may detect a lump, indurated ulcer, friability, and or discolouration. In early disease, high-resolution anoscopy with acetic acid application to the anorectal mucosa improves lesion detection.

MRI {25354914; 29134349} and endoanal ultrasound {28152518} are used to assess local disease. MRI is also useful in assessing treatment response {25354914; 29089827; 29134349} after an appropriate interval {28209296}. Regional lymph node assessment is enhanced by PET, but false positives may occur {28972796; 28280225}.

Most patients are diagnosed in the sixth decade of life or later {26224796}. Cellular immune deficiency contributes to a younger presentation {23042932; 27774311}.

The age-standardized incidence rate of invasive SCC ranges from 0.2 cases per 100 000 person-years in Asia to 1.7 cases per 100 000 person-years in North America and northern Europe {26224796; 24410872; 27789668; 26651444; 25973771}. Rising incidence rates are believed to be related to evolving sexual behaviour and increased duration of HPV infection in HIV-positive patients {23042932; 27774311; 18427149}. The incidence is higher in women and is unrelated to the prevalence of HIV, unlike in men {26224796; 24127500; 26651444; 25973771}.

The etiological relationship between HPV and anal SCC is well established {15241823; 25510243; 9358129}. HPV (most often HPV16) infection underlies 90% of cases {15241823; 22958581}. Multigenotype infection occurs {19838162}. Additional risk factors include cellular immunodeficiency {23042932; 29093575}, anoreceptive intercourse {14682441; 25867258}, coinfection with other sexually transmitted infections {22427679; 29179876}, and cigarette smoking {25867258}. Longstanding perianal Crohn disease has been suggested as a potential risk factor for anal cancer {26938479; 26044314}, but a large study revealed that only 2 of > 2900 such patients developed anal SCC {29199142}.

HPV infection is the main oncogenic driver, and its key oncoproteins are E6 and E7. E6 physically inactivates p53, facilitating survival of cells with genotoxic damage {8207801}. E7 leads to degradation and sequestering of RB1, allowing mutation-bearing cells to continue to proliferate {8840974}. Loss of RB1 function leads to overexpression of p16, which is used diagnostically {12861066}. Additional factors such as immunosuppression {23042932; 29093575; 19960431; 20730855} are required for tumorigenesis, but the specific mechanisms/pathways by which they contribute to tumour development are unknown.
Thickening of the mucosa or a mass may be present, with or without ulceration.

Anal SCC is histologically heterogeneous and often composed of large eosinophilic cells characterized by keratinization. Alternatively, it may resemble urothelial carcinoma. Basaloid SCC refers to a pattern characterized by marked hyperchromasia, scant cytoplasm, and a peripheral palisade of tumour cells around the infiltrating trabeculae. This was previously called cloacogenic carcinoma. Rarely, basaloid tumour cell nests may be accompanied by hyalinization imparting an adenoid cystic–like appearance {26866355; 16327441}. Rarer still is a pattern composed of squamous cells with admixed mucin-containing cells. The descriptive term mucoepidermoid carcinoma is discouraged, to avoid clinical confusion {26866355}. Recognition of these various histological patterns is useful to avoid misdiagnosis, but frequent admixture, subjectivity, lack of biological significance, and the predominance of biopsy-only sampling have contributed to the abandonment of histological subtyping for clinical purposes {10782881; 18724100}.

Verrucous carcinoma (VC) displays exophytic and endophytic growth of bulbous fronds of thickened epithelium with a pushing interface. VC lacks HPV cytopathic effect and severe cytological atypia. Mitoses are rare and basal. On small biopsies, the definitive diagnosis of VC is often impossible and may only be suggested based on clinical information. VC is locally destructive but does not metastasize. In some cases, areas of unequivocal conventional SCC are seen arising in VC. These cases can metastasize and should be diagnosed as conventional SCC. Thorough sampling is prudent before diagnosing VC. Giant condyloma of Buschke–Lowenstein was considered synonymous with VC. However, they are different entities; VC is negative for HPV and giant condyloma is associated with low-risk HPV, viral cytopathic effect, and exophytic growth only {28012208}.

Pseudoepitheliomatous squamous hyperplasia and basal cell carcinomas of the perianal skin may mimic SCC. Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia shows limited cytological atypia and no invasion. An underlying granular cell tumour or syphilis may be identified. Retraction artefact, lack of atypical mitoses, and absence of an in situ component distinguish basal cell carcinoma from SCC {23599161}. A broad range of neoplasms may mimic poorly differentiated SCC. Identification of an in situ component is frequently helpful in SCC diagnosis, but it should be interpreted cautiously, because mimics may involve the surface mucosa, including in a pagetoid manner.

Useful ancillary diagnostic markers for anal squamous cell carcinoma and its mimics are presented in Table #0726.
The cytology of SCC is described in the section Anal squamous dysplasia (intraepithelial neoplasia) section.

Frequent mutations and genomic alterations in the PIK3CA/AKT/mTOR pathway, most commonly in PIK3CA {27052656; 29416628}, have been identified. Overall, the tumour mutation burden is low {29416628}. HPV E6–mediated degradation inactivates p53, so TP53 mutations are typically a feature of HPV-negative SCC {27052656}.

Essential: infiltrating squamous cell clusters and strands with malignant nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm; mitotic activity including atypical forms, intercellular bridges, and variable keratin production.

Note: See Histopathology, above, for other growth patterns of this histologically heterogeneous tumour.

Anal SCC is staged according to the TNM system. Approximately 80% of patients present with the mass localized to the anal mucosa {27048435}. Lymph from the anus drains towards the internal iliac and periaortic nodes or inguinal and femoral lymph nodes. Nodal metastases are detected in approximately 20% of patients {27048435; 23578724}.

Pathological stage is the most important prognostic factor {25239441}. The prognostic value of grade is confounded by stage, and morphological heterogeneity in anal SCC has rendered the value of grade on biopsies questionable {25239441}. Tumour response by imaging correlates with outcome {25354914; 28972796; 27423677}. HIV status does not alter disease-specific outcome, but HIV infection portends more treatment-related toxicity {27774311; 25976897}. PDL1 expression by tumour cells has been identified in approximately half of anal SCC cases {28334399}, and early data indicate encouraging responses to PD1 inhibition {28453692}.
